channel.title: Relational Tech Network Updates
channel.description: Meaningful changes across the relational tech ecosystem -- community tools, neighborhood apps, and civic technology.

item.title: community-supplies: 9 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: The community-supplies platform gained a search feature for finding supplies shared by community members, and a bug in the auto-approval flow was fixed so requests are handled correctly. These improvements make it easier for neighbors in the Sunset and Richmond to find what they need and ensure sharing requests move through the system reliably. Other builders working on mutual aid or resource-sharing tools may find the search and approval patterns here worth a look.

item.title:
community-supplies: Security + UX hardening: approval gate, email leak, explicit membership status
Audit fixes for the
item.description: Community Supplies closed several security gaps that were quietly exposing member email addresses and allowing unapproved users to read the catalog. Members waiting for approval are now properly blocked from accessing shared resources until a steward approves them, and stewards get a clearer view of who is pending versus deactivated. Builders working on multi-community or approval-gated platforms will find the patterns here useful, especially the unified join flow and the explicit membership status field.

item.title: mini-app-starter: Update
item.description: Welcome **mini-app-starter** to the relational tech network! 🎉 This project is bringing a Lovable-style experience to building small, personal mini apps for you and your friends, and we love to see it. So glad to have you here!

item.title: outer-sunset-today: 7 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Outer Sunset Today pushed a round of fixes and updates to their community calendar, including repairs to the event extraction system that pulls local happenings into the platform. More reliable event extraction means fewer missing or broken listings, so neighbors get a more complete and accurate picture of what's going on in the Outer Sunset. If your project aggregates events from outside sources, the patterns here around extraction reliability are worth a look.

item.title: community-guaranteed-income-club: 21 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: The Community Guaranteed Income Club app received a significant round of updates, including a new Directory and Network tab, deployed backend functions, and security fixes. These changes make it easier for neighbors to find and connect with each other through the platform, while the security improvements help protect member data. Builders working on mutual aid or peer funding tools may find the member and admin infrastructure here worth exploring.

item.title: neighboring-recipes: Update

item.title: Local First Auth: README updated
item.description: Local First Auth now supports anonymous accounts, letting people use apps without creating any identity at all. This opens the door for community tools that want to lower the barrier to participation, especially for neighbors who are cautious about sharing personal information or who just want to try something out before committing. It's a meaningful option for mutual aid platforms, civic tools, and any project where trust needs to be built gradually.

item.title: Local First Auth: 3 commits by dmathewwws
item.description: Local First Auth now lets users edit their profiles and sign in with anonymous accounts, alongside a new 2.3.0 release. Anonymous accounts are a meaningful step for community tools where people may want to participate without sharing identifying information, lowering the barrier to entry for privacy-conscious users. Builders working on mutual aid platforms, civic engagement tools, or any app where trust-building happens gradually now have more flexible options for how people show up.

item.title: community-supplies: 8 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: The community-supplies platform for Sunset and Richmond got a significant round of improvements, including authentication and a community guard to make sure only the right people can access the supplies-sharing features. This kind of member verification helps build trust in sharing systems, ensuring that resources stay within the community they were built for. Other builders working on mutual aid or resource-sharing tools may find the community access control approach worth adapting for their own projects.

item.title: outer-sunset-today: 6 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Outer Sunset Today fixed a bug that was causing event times to display incorrectly during Daylight Saving Time in the Pacific timezone. This kind of time handling issue can quietly cause community members to show up at the wrong time, so getting it right is a real win for anyone relying on the calendar. Other builders working with local event times across timezone boundaries may want to take note of this as a common pitfall.

item.title: outer-sunset-today: 8 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Outer Sunset Today added Far Out West as a new source to its event scraper, bringing more local happenings into the community calendar automatically. This means residents get a fuller picture of what's going on in the neighborhood without anyone having to manually add events. The team also simplified the interface by removing the alerts system and its call-to-action, streamlining the experience for visitors.

item.title: outer-sunset-today: 12 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Outer Sunset Today added a source URL field to events, giving each listing a direct link back to where it came from. This makes it easier for neighbors to verify event details, find the original organizer, and trust the information they see. Other calendar projects tracking events from multiple sources may find this a useful pattern for attribution and transparency.

item.title: Local First Auth: 2 commits by dmathewwws
item.description: Local First Auth now gives each web app its own unique identity for each user, so a person's activity on one neighborhood tool can't be linked to their activity on another. This is a meaningful step forward for community platforms that want to protect residents from cross-site tracking without asking them to manage passwords or accounts. Builders working on privacy-respecting civic tools now have a cleaner foundation to build on.

item.title: Local First Auth: v3.0.0
item.description: Local First Auth has released version 3.0, a major update to this tool that lets web apps handle sign-in entirely on the user's device, with no passwords or outside services involved. For community tech builders, this means it's easier to add privacy-respecting authentication to neighborhood tools without relying on big tech identity providers or maintaining a backend server. If your project handles sensitive community data and you want to keep control local, this release is worth exploring.

item.title: local-first-auth-simulator: 2 commits by dmathewwws
item.description: The local-first-auth-simulator has released version 2.0.0, with a significant update that ties cryptographic key derivation to specific origins. This means developers testing Local First Auth mini-apps now get more realistic and secure simulated environments, where keys behave the way they would in production across different hosting contexts. If your project uses Local First Auth, this tool just got more trustworthy as a testing companion.

item.title: community-supplies: 32 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Community Supplies, a supplies-sharing site for the Sunset and Richmond neighborhoods, received a significant round of updates including a new Request Board feature, dark mode support, onboarding demo data, and clearer calls to action. The Request Board is a meaningful addition, giving community members a dedicated place to ask for what they need rather than only browsing what's available. Builders working on mutual aid or resource-sharing platforms may find the onboarding and request-posting patterns here worth a look.

item.title: cozy-corner: 15 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Cozy Corner, the neighbor hub for 48th Ave in the Outer Sunset, added a full Block Party 2026 signup experience, including a dedicated page, a registration form with friendly emoji labels, and a translated version of the page for non-English speakers. This makes it easier for more neighbors to learn about and sign up for the block party, regardless of language background. Other builders working on hyperlocal event signups or multilingual community pages may find this a useful reference for keeping things simple and welcoming.

item.title: sunset-wave: Add About page and improve site navigation
item.description: Sunset Wave now has a dedicated About page and a consistent navigation bar, giving visitors a clear path to understand the project, learn how the microgrant gathering model works, and take action as a host or participant. This kind of welcoming onboarding layer makes the difference between a tool that only insiders can figure out and one that genuinely invites a whole neighborhood in. The new 'How it works' overview and host-vs-join call-to-action cards are patterns other builders might borrow for their own community platforms.

item.title: sunset-wave: Readability, mobile UX, map labeling, and README
item.description: Sunset Wave shipped a round of accessibility and mobile improvements, including better color contrast across the interface, larger touch targets, a friendlier bottom-sheet dialog, and an edge-to-edge map that works well on phones. The map's row labels now name both cross streets, making it easier for neighbors to find their block, and the grid has a descriptive aria-label for screen reader users. The project also gained a real README that explains how the tool works, how to run it, and where it came from.

item.title: sunset-wave: README updated
item.description: Sunset Wave rolled out a new visual identity, including a custom wordmark with hand-drawn SVG icons, a warmer color palette, rounder shapes, and a lowercase voice that carries through every button, heading, and nav label on the site. The cohesive look and feel helps the project present a more welcoming, neighborhood-native personality, and the updated color choices were tested to meet accessibility contrast standards throughout. Other builders working on community-facing tools may find the approach to voice and visual consistency worth borrowing.

item.title: sunset-wave: New visual identity: sunset wave wordmark, icons, palette, lowercase voice
item.description: Sunset Wave rolled out a new visual identity across their whole site, with a rounded typeface, a warmer color palette, custom wave and waving-hand icons, and a consistent lowercase voice throughout the interface. All text colors were checked to meet accessibility contrast standards on the new background, so the friendlier look doesn't come at a cost to readability. The printable neighborhood invitation got the same treatment, making the whole project feel cohesive from screen to paper.
